interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fourteen small screens on the quadratic formula. Each picture is a parabola, a sketch drawn from its rule, with a dashed upright line, its axis, at x = −b ÷ 2a, and two equal arrows from the axis along the x-axis out to the roots, each √(b² − 4ac) ÷ 2a long (its size, when a is negative). A readout shows b² − 4ac, with what it means on the line below it: two real and distinct roots, one repeated real root or no real roots. Screens: 1 shows y = x² + 6x + 2 from lesson 4, axis at −3, arrows √7, about 2.65, out to −0.35 and −5.65, readout 28; 2 asks for the roots of x² + 6x + 5 = 0 from its arrows of 2; 3 builds the formula line by line by completing the square with letters; 4 is a spot-the-slip: a worked answer to x² + 6x + 5 = 0 that put only the square root over 2a and got −4 and −8, and you pick the line that slipped; 5 works x² + 6x + 2 = 0 through the formula, √28 = 2√7, giving −3 ± √7 again; 6 asks for b² − 4ac in 2x² − 4x − 6 = 0; 7 lets you drag y = x² + 6x + c up and down, c from 0 to 12, while the readout 36 − 4c falls, the arrows shrink, meet at −3 when c is 9 and the readout 0, and vanish past it, where the readout says 'no real roots' in ink; 8 asks about x² + 2x + 5 = 0; 9 gives handles for a, b and c, opening on −x² + 4x + 10, an upside-down U with its axis at 2 and arrows √14, about 3.74; 10 asks what 4x² − 12x + 9 = 0 has: two real and distinct roots, one repeated real root or no real roots; 11 works OpenStax's firework, 4.90t² − 14.3t − 20.0 = 0, through the formula, b² − 4ac = 204.49 + 392 = 596.49, to about 3.95 s and −1.03 s, says OpenStax prints 3.96 s, probably from unrounded numbers, and that a calculator's equation solver checks the roots; 12 asks for the roots of x² − 7x + 10 = 0, which factorises, where one wrong pick, just 5, drops the ±, and its Why? shows the formula agreeing; 13 asks for the roots of 3x² + 5x − 1 = 0 to two decimal places, which has no whole-number pair, so the formula is the quick way, and its Why? puts 0.18 back and says to type the bottom in brackets on a calculator; 14 asks which of x² − 4x + 3, x² − 4x + 4 and x² − 4x + 5 has no real roots, and ends by saying the roots it rules out are complex numbers, for the Complex numbers course. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to pick one answer from three; after Check, a puzzle's working appears beneath its buttons. On the screens that ask for roots, a wrong pick puts its number back into the rule and shows it does not give 0, or, for the pick that drops the ±, that the other root gives 0 too.

explain.text:
The [[quadratic formula]] gives the answers to any quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 that has them: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a.[^1] In words: minus b, plus or minus the square root of b squared take away 4ac, all over 2a. It is lesson 4's completing the square done once with letters, so you need not do it each time, and it reads as a centre, −b ÷ 2a, with the two roots the same distance either side.

Here is where it comes from. a is not 0, or there would be no x² and no quadratic. Take a out of the x² and x terms: a(x² + (b ÷ a)x) + c. Half of b ÷ a is b ÷ 2a, so the corner is (b ÷ 2a)², and it comes off a times, which is b² ÷ 4a. That gives a(x + b ÷ 2a)² + c − b² ÷ 4a.[^2] Set it to 0 and take the plain part across: a(x + b ÷ 2a)² = b² ÷ 4a − c, and since c is 4ac ÷ 4a, that is (b² − 4ac) ÷ 4a. Divide both sides by a: (x + b ÷ 2a)² = (b² − 4ac) ÷ 4a². A square equals this number only when what is squared is its positive or its negative square root, so x + b ÷ 2a = ±√(b² − 4ac) ÷ 2a (√(4a²) is 2a or −2a, whichever is positive, and the ± covers both). Take b ÷ 2a across: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a. Check it on lesson 4's x² + 6x + 2 = 0: a = 1, b = 6, c = 2, so b² − 4ac = 36 − 8 = 28, and √28 = √4 × √7 = 2√7, as in Powers and roots. So x = (−6 ± 2√7) ÷ 2 = −3 ± √7, about −0.35 or −5.65, the same as before. The ± is two answers, and dropping it loses one: x² + 6x + 5 = 0 with only the + gives x = −1, yet −5 works too, since 25 − 30 + 5 = 0.

Split the formula and it is a picture: x = −b ÷ 2a ± √(b² − 4ac) ÷ 2a. The first part is the centre, the line of symmetry from lesson 4, halfway between the roots. The second is the spread, the same distance out to each root, which the two arrows show. The spread rests on b² − 4ac, the number under the square root, called the [[discriminant]].[^3] Drag y = x² + 6x + c up by raising c and the discriminant, 36 − 4c, falls, so the arrows shrink. Lesson 4 says why: x² + 6x + c = 0 is (x + 3)² = 9 − c, and 36 − 4c is just 4 × (9 − c), so lifting the curve asks the square to make a smaller and smaller number. At c = 9 that number is 0: the arrows have no length, the two roots meet at x = −3, and the curve just touches the axis, because its lowest point, c − 9, is 0. That is one [[repeated root]], because x² + 6x + 9 is the perfect square (x + 3)², so both brackets give −3. Lift it to c = 11 and the discriminant is −8. No number on the number line squares to a negative, so −8 has no square root there and the curve never reaches the axis. The roots it has then are complex, numbers off the number line,[^3] which wait for the Complex numbers course.

The formula works just as well on numbers that are not whole. OpenStax finds a firework shell's time in the air from 4.90t² − 14.3t − 20.0 = 0, with t in seconds, so a = 4.90, b = −14.3 and c = −20.0.[^4] Then b² − 4ac = 204.49 + 392 = 596.49, whose square root is about 24.42, and t = (14.3 ± 24.42) ÷ 9.8, about 3.95 or −1.03. OpenStax prints 3.96 s, probably because it worked from unrounded figures; with the numbers as printed the formula gives 3.95. The negative time is before the launch, so OpenStax sets it aside,[^5] as lesson 7 takes up. A calculator's equation solver gives the same two roots: a quick check on your working, though it shows none of it.

**x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a, and b² − 4ac tells you before you start whether there are two real and distinct roots, one repeated real root or no real roots.[^3]**

analogy.text: Say a resistor is marked 100 Ω with a tolerance of 5 Ω. Its two limits are 95 Ω and 105 Ω: a centre, and the same step either side. The formula gives the two roots the same way, a centre −b ÷ 2a and a step √(b² − 4ac) ÷ 2a either side, and a step of 0 leaves one value.
analogy.breaks: A tolerance covers every value between its limits, while a quadratic is zero only at the two ends; between them, when a is positive, its graph dips below the axis. And a tolerance always exists, while the step comes from a square root, so when b² − 4ac is negative there is no real step at all.

practice.text:
- Rearrange to ax² + bx + c = 0, with 0 alone on one side.
- Write down a, b and c with their signs.
- Work out b² − 4ac first. b² is never negative, and −4ac turns positive when just one of a and c is negative (with both negative, a = −1 and c = −2, it is −8).
- Read it in SQA's words: positive, two real and distinct roots; 0, one repeated real root; negative, no real roots, so stop there.[^6]
- Put the whole top, −b ± the square root, over 2a.
- Check each root by putting it back into the rule: it should give 0, or very nearly 0 if you rounded.

**Rule of thumb:** If a pair for factorising comes quickly, factorise; if not, use the formula, which works on every quadratic and tells you when there are no real roots. The two roots must average to −b ÷ 2a, which is a quick check.

**Worked example:** Lesson 4 found −x² + 4x + 10 = −(x − 2)² + 14. Solve −x² + 4x + 10 = 0 with the formula: a = −1, b = 4, c = 10. b² − 4ac = 16 − 4 × (−1) × 10 = 16 + 40 = 56, positive, so two roots. √56 = 2√14, about 7.48. x = (−4 ± 7.48) ÷ (−2), so x is about −1.74 or 5.74. They average to 2, which is −b ÷ 2a = −4 ÷ −2, the highest point lesson 4 found. Check x = 5.74: −32.95 + 22.96 + 10 = 0.01, which is 0 but for the rounding.

**Common mistakes**
- Dropping the ±, so x² + 6x + 5 = 0 gives only x = −1. −5 works too.
- Putting only the square root over 2a, so x² + 6x + 5 = 0 gives −6 ± 2, which is −4 or −8. At x = −4 the rule gives −3, not 0.
- Squaring a minus b to a minus: in 2x² − 4x − 6, b² is 16, not −16.
- Losing the sign of −4ac: with a = 2 and c = −6, −4ac is +48, so b² − 4ac is 64, not −32.
- Finding roots from a negative discriminant. x² + 2x + 5 has 4 − 20 = −16, so no real roots; 1 and −3 each give 8, not 0.

checks.label: The quadratic formula for ax^2 + bx + c = 0 is x = (−b ± √(b^2 − 4ac)) ÷ 2a: on every screen, and at every a, b and c tried on the handles, each root it gives makes the rule 0, and the roots drawn are exactly those

Completing the square converts ax^2 + bx + c to a(x + b/(2a))^2 + (c − b^2/(4a)): for every screen's rule and every a, b and c tried on the handles, the two agree at every x tried, and at each root the bracket squared is (b^2 − 4ac)/(4a^2)

The discriminant distinguishes two distinct real roots, one repeated real root, or non-real complex roots only: on every screen and setting tried, the picture draws two roots and two equal arrows when b² − 4ac is above zero, one root and arrows of no length at zero, and no roots or arrows below zero, and the readout says which
Both arrows start on the dashed axis at x = −b ÷ 2a and are equal, each √(b² − 4ac) ÷ 2a long (its size when a is negative), so the axis sits halfway between the roots, which average to −b ÷ 2a

On y = x² + 6x + c, raising c from 0 to 12 takes the readout 36 − 4c down by 4 each step, from 36 to −12; the arrows shrink every step, meet at x = −3 when c is 9, where the readout is 0, and from c = 10 there are none and it says no real roots

Every puzzle accepts only its right answer, worked out from its rule; each wrong pick of roots, put back into the rule, does not give 0 (or, dropping the ±, gives one root and misses the other) while the right ones do, and each hint quotes the rule's own value there

The worked numbers: 36 − 8 = 28 with arrows of 2.65 to −0.35 and −5.65; 36 − 20 = 16 with arrows of 2 to −1 and −5, where 1 and 5 give 12 and 60 and the slip's −4 and −8 give −3 and 21; √28 = 2√7, about 5.29; 16 + 48 = 64, not −32 or −64; 36 − 4c from 36 to −12; 4 − 20 = −16; 16 + 40 = 56 with arrows of 3.74; 144 − 144 = 0 at 1.5; 49 − 40 = 9; the firework's 204.49 + 392 = 596.49 with arrows of 2.49 to 3.95 and −1.03; 25 + 12 = 37 with roots 0.18 and −1.85; and the practice check −32.95 + 22.96 + 10 = 0.01 at x = 5.74

Before Check a puzzle hides the curve, the roots and b² − 4ac; after a right answer the curve is drawn whole with its axis, arrows and roots, and a wrong pick puts its own numbers back into the rule, in red
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s

applied.problem: "There is nothing to take the square root of" is false (−8 is there; it has no square root on the number line, and has complex ones); "Everything rests on b² − 4ac" overstates it, as the centre −b ÷ 2a does not; and the bold "two roots" drops the quote's "real".

"Roots are shown to two decimal places, so putting one back gives very nearly 0, not exactly" is false for the whole-number roots on screens 2, 6, 10 and 11 (−1, −5, 3, 1.5, 5, 2), which give exactly 0.

"A wrong pick puts its number back into the rule" cannot hold on screens 6, 10 and 13, whose picks are discriminants, kinds of root or rules, not roots; and "which only the formula finds easily" overstates it, since completing the square finds 3x² + 5x − 1 = 0 too.
